title: Tortilla Chips 300g

drivers.name: Price increase to $3.97
drivers.evidence: Two recent weeks at $3.97 averaged 90.5 units (27% below baseline median). This is consistent and exceeds ordinary week noise (29%). No prior price increase at this level, but trend is clear.

adjustment.analysis: The baseline median is 124.2. No events are scheduled. The price is increased to $3.97 (+3.7% vs regular $3.83), and recent weeks show a clear negative response: the two weeks at $3.97 (2026-09-28 and 2026-10-05) averaged 90.5 units, 27% below baseline. This is consistent with past price sensitivity. The noise-adjusted effect of price increases is not directly available, but the observed drop is robust and exceeds ordinary week noise (29%). No promotion or event is planned, and Halloween had no historical uplift. The classical model’s 1.00 multiplier ignores the price effect. Adjust downward for price increase.

brief:
PRODUCT: Tortilla Chips 300g | category Snacks | Store #12 (Austin, TX)
TARGET WEEK: 2026-10-19 to 2026-10-25 (2 weeks after the last week with sales data)

KNOWN PLAN FOR THE TARGET WEEK:
  events: none
  shelf price: 3.97 (+3.7% vs regular price 3.83)

STATISTICAL BASELINE (exponential smoothing of recent sales; it ignores events, promotions and prices):
  median 124.2 | 5%-95%: 77.7 - 200.1 | 10%-90%: 89.1 - 170.1

In the evidence below, 'vs baseline' = actual units / what this same baseline predicted for that week.
It is the multiplier that would have been right, so it maps directly onto median_multiplier.
This product's ordinary weeks already swing about +/-29% around the baseline, so a past effect smaller than that, seen only a few times, is mostly noise. The
'noise-adjusted estimate' is the effect shrunk toward x1.0 for that noise and the number of sightings.
